1 Deductions — pick a series in the bar to give it its own values; everything else in this section follows it
Deductions for
Sliding systems
How sliding systems work

Pick 2 Track, 2.5 Track or 3 Track on a window and its counts come from here automatically, along with that system's own deductions (the frame, shutter and mesh profiles differ between systems). Deductions start equal across systems — set each to your profile chart. Shutters are the frames cut from the shutter profile; Glass panes is how many of them hold glass, and any left over carry a mesh net (so a 3 Track is 3 shutters, 2 glass + 1 mesh, with a mesh type to choose). A shutter that carries mesh — the 3 Track's Al/SS mesh shutter — is cut from the mesh profile at the same size as the glass shutters, and listed as Mesh profile (3 Track) on the BOM with its code (set Mesh shutters cut from to the shutter profile if a system's mesh shutter is an ordinary shutter). Separate mesh frames — like the mesh on a 2.5 Track, which is 2 glass shutters + 1 mesh frame — are cut from the 2.5 Track's own, different mesh profile (Mesh profile (2.5 Track) on the BOM), on their own sticks. If every shutter on your 3 Track holds glass, set its Glass panes to 3.

A profile ticked here is cut 2 sides at one shot — two bars clamped together: each window's matching sides (top & bottom, left & right) are paired, and every cutting pattern is cut on bar A and bar B at once. A mullion or transom is a single piece, so it is usually left unticked.

Mesh rolls & nesting

Widths of the mesh rolls you stock, in feet. Mesh Nesting lays the nets out on these rolls, turning a net 90° where that saves mesh, and picks the roll (or mix of rolls) that wastes least.
4 Window types & lists

Window types (the Type dropdown in Window Schedule)

Sliding takes its shutters and mesh from its Track (see Sliding systems above). Every other type sets them here: how many shutters, how many separate mesh frames, and what fills it — Glass, or Louvers (louvre blades: no glass pane is cut, and no beading).
Fixed, Openable, Ventilator and Ventilator with fan are built in — ventilators have no shutter, no mesh and louvers (their glass is in the louvers, so no glass pane is cut or nested); their frame is cut from the ventilator profile — its own sticks in Profile Nesting and its own line on the BOM. A type you add can be removed once no window uses it; to rename one, add the new name and remove the old.

5 Codes & prices — for the BOM and the costing

Profile codes, weights & prices (codes on the BOM; weight × price for the costing)

For each profile — frame, shutter, beading, the two mesh profiles, the ventilator profile and mullion / transom — its code, its weight in kg per metre and its price in ₹ per kg. A profile with both costs sticks × stick length × kg/m × ₹/kg on BOM & Costing; one without keeps a price-per-stick box there. Each brand's All series row is used by every series that has no value of its own (and by windows with no series). Brands and series come from the Type lists; renaming one there keeps its values. These numbers can also be typed on the cost sheet —

Glass & mesh prices

₹ per sqft for each type in the Type lists. Glass is costed on the stock sheets you buy (offcuts included), mesh on the roll you pull. The same prices as on the cost sheet —
6 Hardware — counted from your windows onto the BOM, with its prices

Hardware (listed on the BOM)

Each item is counted for the windows it applies to: Qty × the per count of each window × its window quantity. For example "Roller · 2 · per glass shutter · Sliding" gives a 2 Track window 4 rollers. Items with the same name, code and unit are added up; pieces round up to whole numbers, metres to the next 0.1 m. Screws each is how many screws fit one piece (or pair / set): the BOM shows each fitting's screws and the total per screw type. Set the code from your supplier's list; remove what you don't use. The prices are the same as on the cost sheet —

Cutting list

The order spec, then every window’s cut sizes in mm.

How it works

The order spec, then each window's cut sizes in the Full Table. Profile brand, colour, glass and mesh type are stated once at the top and shown on a window's line only where they vary.

Profile nesting

How each stick is cut, the fewest sticks first. Cut the longest pieces first.

How it works

Each stick starts with the longest piece left and is filled with the combination of remaining pieces that leaves the least waste (saw kerf included — at 45° the blade takes √2 × its width along the bar); several methods are compared and the one needing the fewest sticks is used. Pieces of the same profile, brand and colour share sticks. Cut bigger first, smaller later: the sticks are in order from the one with the biggest pieces to the one with the smallest, and on every stick the longest piece is cut first. When the profile is cut at 45°, each piece is drawn with its mitred ends — long point along the top — and the small triangles between pieces are the offcut.

Glass

The glass for each window, then how each sheet is cut, on the stock size that wastes least.

How it works

Each sheet is laid out for guillotine cutting — every cut runs edge to edge, as glass is scored and snapped — on whichever stock size wastes least, trying several layouts and keeping the one that needs the fewest sheets. A pane marked ⟲ lies turned 90° on the sheet (for patterned glass, untick "Panes may be turned" in ).

Glass requirement — from each window’s shutter size (or its frame size, for Fixed)

Sheets — how each stock sheet is cut

Mesh nesting

How the mesh nets are cut from your rolls.

How it works

How the mesh nets are cut from the rolls. Each cut is a length pulled off the roll and cut straight across; the nets in it are then cut apart. Nets may be turned 90° to save mesh. W = window number; sizes are each net's width × height, and a "turned" net lies sideways on the roll.

Expenses

What you pay out, and what each order really cost you.

How it works

Type each amount you pay and pick what it was for. Material, Labour & wages and Transport & site are often for one job: pick its order under For, and that order shows what it cost against its sale. Rent, power and tea go to Shop / general.

To add quickly: tap one of the expenses under Again to fill every box the way it was last time; or type an item or a payee you have paid before, and the rest fills in by itself (last ₹… puts in the last amount). Monthly bills brings back last month’s shop bills — rent, power, internet — to add in one go. Click an expense in the list to change it; ✕ removes it, and Undo puts it back. To remove several, press Select, tick them (or Tick all) and Remove. A category in the month’s card shows only that category.

Besides the four built-in categories you can add your own: + New beside them, or Edit categories to rename or remove one. A category removed passes its expenses to Shop overheads.

Staff salaries: add each worker with their monthly salary. + Advance records money given ahead — it is taken off that month’s salary — and Pay pays what is left; both are Labour & wages expenses in the list, with the worker as Paid to. Salary not paid is still owed the month after, and an advance bigger than the month’s salary is taken off the next month. Click a worker to change their salary (a raise counts from the month shown on), add an extra or a cut for one month (overtime, a bonus, leave), see or remove that month’s advances and payments, or mark that they left.

Profit so far is the order’s sale before GST (its quote, or the total agreed on ) less what you spent on it. The amounts you type are what you paid, GST included. The estimate is the order’s cost on . Expenses cover the whole business: uPVC and door orders are shown together here, whichever side is open — pick uPVC orders or Door orders under For, or uPVC / Doors above the order table, to see one side. Expenses are kept in this browser with your orders, and Back up all data saves them too.

Production PlanningDoor Production Planning

Confirmed orders through your stations, day by day, against their due dates.Confirmed door orders on the door line, day by day, against their due dates.

How it works

Confirmed and In-production orders flow through your shop — Cutting, Welding, Cleaning & fitting, Glazing, QC & dispatch — in sequence, each station at its own capacity a day, from today, skipping holidays and counting only what is not yet done. What a station finishes today reaches the next one tomorrow. Each order gets its start, finish and ready date against its due date; the station with the most days of work is the bottleneck. Give each order a priority — 1 urgent … 5 least: the plan takes priority 1 first. Best sequence keeps the priorities and reorders the Confirmed orders within each so the fewest are late. Below: the timeline, each day's work at every station, and the material the plan needs.

Confirmed and In-production door orders go through the door line, one after another, at its doors a day — from today, skipping holidays, counting only the doors not yet made. Each order gets its start, finish and ready date against its due date. Give each order a priority — 1 urgent … 5 least. Best sequence keeps the priorities and reorders the Confirmed orders within each so the fewest are late. The uPVC windows are planned on their own, on the uPVC side.

Nesting compares several methods and keeps the one that uses the least material — best-fill stick packing for profile, guillotine layouts for glass, strip packing on rolls for mesh. Practical results, not a guaranteed optimum.
